title: Living ashtpadi 13

cards: Try counting, for one lunch break, how much of the talk around you is about people who aren't there. Who's dating whom. Who got the promotion and didn't deserve it.
What the neighbor is doing with that yard. Most of it isn't cruel. It's the easy, warm currency of being together, and that's what makes it hard: gossip usually isn't a decision.
It's a habit of the tongue, running ahead of us. The thirteenth ashtpadi warned about slander of the holy. Living it means watching its smaller cousin, the one that shows up at lunch.

teach.b: Gurbani's word for the tongue is rasnaa, and it sits right beside ras: taste, juice, flavor. The tongue is the taster, and the Gurus play with that. What the tongue keeps tasting, it gets a taste for.
Hymns speak of a tongue that savors the Name, that has found the sweetest flavor and wants nothing else.

teach.h: A TASTE FOR THE NAME, OR FOR FAULTS.
teach.b: The opposite is a tongue with a taste for other people's faults, going back for more.

teach.h: PHIKAA: HARSH WORDS MAKE YOU BLAND.
teach.b: Guru Nanak puts it bluntly in Asa di Var, the hymn we met a few days ago: speaking harsh, tasteless words, the body and mind themselves become tasteless. The word is phikaa: bland, flat, insipid, like food with no salt.
Unkind talk doesn't only wound someone else; it drains the flavor out of the person talking. Put beside the thirteenth ashtpadi, the shape is clear. Slander of the holy stains the mind.
Everyday gossip, its small cousin, flattens it. Both start on the tongue. So why guard the tongue rather than the thoughts?
Because the tongue is where a passing thought becomes a habit. A thought about someone's faults can drift by. Said out loud, it gets an audience, a laugh, a reply, and comes back stronger tomorrow.

teach.h: A GATE AT THE END OF THE PATH.
teach.b: Guarding the tongue is a gate at the end of the path: thoughts may still wander up to it, but they don't get out into the world.
And a gate is a small thing to build: one changed subject, at one lunch table.

how: Gurbani returns often to the rasnaa, the tongue, and to the sweetness of speaking the Name; Sukhmani's warnings on slander and Guru Nanak's line on harsh words are read as a guard on gossip.

o: the breath, drawn in during prayer
a sweet hymn sung at evening prayer
the tongue, the part of us that tastes

p: where a thought becomes a habit

s: Guru Nanak says harsh words leave the speaker's own body and mind flat
in Asa di Var, speaking phikaa words makes body and mind phikaa.
Gurbani's word for tongue has nothing to do with taste
rasnaa sits beside ras, taste, and the Gurus play on the pair.
this lesson treats gossip mainly as a deliberate decision
it calls gossip a habit of the tongue, running ahead of us.

games.q: at lunch, talk turns to a coworker who isn't there. you want to live ashtpadi 13. what's your move?
o: join in, but keep it mild.
change the subject, or say something good about them.
games.why: guard the tongue: close the gate gently. a lecture just turns the gossip toward you, and joining in feeds the taste.

practice: Close your mouth gently and let the tongue lie soft against the floor of your mouth, pressing nowhere, and notice how much it wants to move, even in silence, shaping tiny words. Each time it starts, let it go soft again.
If you pray, you can let it hold one word only, Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Rasnaa, the tongue, the taster. It can learn a taste for the Name or for faults, and harsh words leave the speaker phikaa, flavorless.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rasnaa, the tongue, the taster; Gurbani plays it against ras, taste.

carryVoice: Your line: guard the tongue. The tongue learns what it tastes. Day four hundred eighty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok of Guru Nanak on phikaa words (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473)
Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 13 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279–280)
